title: Integration of UAV-based infrared thermography with building information modeling and digital twins for infrastructure inspection: a review
abstract: Abstract Unmanned aerial vehicle–based infrared thermography (UAV-IRT) has emerged as a promising approach for non-contact infrastructure inspection, enabling thermal diagnostics across large and difficult-to-access built-environment assets. At the same time, the Architecture, Engineering, Construction, and Facility Management (AEC/FM) industry is increasingly adopting digital technologies such as Building Information Modeling (BIM) and digital twins (DTs) to support data-driven asset management and lifecycle decision-making. However, thermal inspection outputs are often treated as isolated datasets rather than interoperable information linked with digital asset models, limiting their value for monitoring and predictive maintenance and constraining their integration into digital asset management workflows. This study presents a review of research at the intersection of UAV-IRT, BIM, and DT technologies. Based on a structured literature screening of 110 publications, this study covers UAV-enabled inspection, thermal data processing, multimodal sensing, and digital model integration. The review synthesizes research across four themes: UAV-IRT applications, thermal data processing and AI-assisted anomaly detection, BIM-based integration approaches, and digital-twin-enabled monitoring frameworks. The analysis reveals fragmentation across sensing, data processing, and integration workflows, highlighting key challenges that hinder scalable deployment in practical infrastructure inspection and management applications. The paper further discusses key directions for future research, including workflow standardization, multimodal sensing integration, AI-enabled decision support, scalable DT ecosystems, and workforce development. The findings demonstrate how UAV-IRT can support asset management by enabling proactive maintenance and improving inspection efficiency by reducing unnecessary inspection cycles and minimizing redundant field operations. These improvements lower resource consumption and operational costs while supporting more effective lifecycle management of infrastructure systems.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Rapid advances in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and infrared thermography (IRT) have substantially expanded the capabilities of non-contact inspection and thermal diagnostics in the built environment, particularly for large-scale and hard-to-access infrastructure systems. UAV-mounted thermal sensors enable rapid, flexible, and large-area data collection while reducing the time, labor, and safety constraints associated with conventional manual inspection methods [ 26 ,  39 ,  78 ,  86 ]. In building and infrastructure applications, UAV-IRT has been used to detect thermal leakage, moisture intrusion, facade anomalies, roof defects, and subsurface deterioration, demonstrating strong potential for energy auditing, condition assessment, and defect identification and contributing to improved energy efficiency and reduced operational resource consumption in buildings and infrastructure systems [ 23 ,  24 ,  68 ,  72 ,  77 ,  111 ]. Recent review studies have highlighted the rapid development of UAV-based infrared thermography for building envelope thermal performance assessment, emphasizing its advantages in large-scale inspection, rapid data acquisition, and non-destructive evaluation of building systems (D. Zhang et al., [ 115 ]).

At the same time, the Architecture, Engineering, Construction, and Facility Management (AEC/FM) industry is undergoing a broader digital transformation driven by Building Information Modeling (BIM), digital twins (DTs), and data-centric asset management approaches. BIM has evolved from a design and coordination platform into an information-rich environment that supports inspection documentation, facility management, and lifecycle decision-making by enabling data-driven evaluation of asset conditions and prioritization of maintenance actions, while DTs further extend this capability by enabling dynamic model updating, condition monitoring, and predictive maintenance [ 63 ,  65 ,  80 ,  95 ]. As infrastructure systems become increasingly complex and performance-oriented, the ability to connect inspection data with semantically structured digital models has become a critical requirement for scalable and intelligent asset management. From an asset management perspective, integrating UAV-IRT with BIM and DTs can reduce inspection costs, enhance data traceability, and support more informed and efficient maintenance planning, thereby supporting more sustainable asset lifecycle management by reducing unnecessary material replacement and minimizing energy losses associated with inefficient maintenance strategies.

Within this context, UAV-IRT is especially promising because it provides spatially distributed thermal information that can reveal defects and performance abnormalities not easily captured through visible imaging alone [ 79 ,  90 ]. Recent studies have also shown growing interest in integrating thermal imagery with photogrammetry, 3D reconstruction, BIM environments, and DT frameworks to create more informative and operationally useful inspection workflows ([ 36 ,  52 ,  56 ,  80 ,  81 ,  87 ,  93 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 107 ] b; [ 112 ]). Such integration can move thermal inspection beyond standalone image interpretation toward model-linked defect localization, automated documentation, and decision support across the asset lifecycle, with the potential to enhance long-term infrastructure resilience and sustainability performance.

However, despite these advances, UAV-IRT data are still frequently used as isolated inspection outputs rather than as interoperable components of a broader digital inspection ecosystem. In many applications, thermal images or orthomosaics remain detached from asset semantics, maintenance databases, and model-based management workflows, limiting their long-term value for monitoring, prioritization, and predictive analysis [ 7 ,  20 ,  71 ,  91 ]. Practical challenges such as sensor calibration, image registration, multimodal data fusion, geometric accuracy, interoperability, and semantic mapping continue to hinder the seamless integration of UAV-IRT outputs into BIM and DT environments ([ 14 ,  20 ,  35 ,  91 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 112  ], Zhang, [ 105 ] a).

Several review studies have examined important parts of this landscape, but mostly in a fragmented manner. However, most existing reviews focus on individual components of the workflow such as UAV inspection technologies, infrared thermography applications, or BIM-based inspection systems, rather than examining how thermal sensing, multimodal data fusion, and DT ecosystems can be integrated into a unified digital inspection pipeline. Prior reviews have addressed UAV applications in the built environment [ 78 ], robotic and drone-based inspection systems [ 26 ,  41 ,  75 ], infrared thermography and thermal diagnostics for buildings (D. Zhang et al., [ 110 ], and infrastructure systems [ 44 ], thermal–3D data fusion and thermal point clouds [ 79 ,  90 ], and UAV–BIM integration for visual inspection workflows [ 10 ,  106 ]. These studies provide valuable foundations, yet they generally focus on one of three perspectives in isolation: UAV-enabled inspection, thermal sensing and analysis, or digital model integration. A comprehensive review that specifically synthesizes how UAV-based infrared thermography can be integrated into BIM and DT ecosystems for intelligent inspection and lifecycle decision support remains limited.

Accordingly, this study presents a structured review and research roadmap for UAV-IRT integration within BIM and DT workflows in the built environment. Rather than treating UAV sensing, thermal analysis, and digital asset modeling as separate research streams, this review examines their intersections across inspection applications, thermal data processing, AI-assisted anomaly detection, multimodal fusion, BIM linkage, and DT development. The goal is not only to summarize the current state of knowledge, but also to identify the key technical, analytical, and organizational barriers that must be addressed to enable scalable and operationally meaningful UAV-IRT-enabled digital inspection systems.
The main contributions of this study are summarized as follows:

to synthesize UAV-IRT applications relevant to infrastructure and building inspection to review thermal data processing and AI-based anomaly detection methods used in UAV-IRT workflows to analyze existing approaches for integrating thermal inspection outputs into BIM and DT environments to identify major research gaps related to sensing, data fusion, interoperability, and implementation to propose a future research roadmap toward scalable UAV-IRT-enabled DTs for intelligent inspection and decision support

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section  2  presents the theoretical foundations of UAV-based infrared thermography, BIM, DTs, and digital inspection workflows. Section  3  describes the review methodology and literature classification framework. Section  4  summarizes UAV-IRT applications in infrastructure inspection. Sect.  5  examines integration pathways between UAV-IRT, BIM, and DTs. Section   6  provides a critical evaluation and research synthesis of the reviewed literature. Section  7  discusses current challenges and research gaps. Section  8  proposes future research directions, followed by conclusions in Sect.   9 .

sections.heading: Principles of UAV-based infrared thermography
paragraphs: Infrared thermography (IRT) is a non-contact and non-destructive sensing technique that detects infrared radiation emitted by an object and converts it into a thermal image representing surface temperature distribution. Because all objects above absolute zero emit infrared radiation, variations in emitted energy can be interpreted as surface temperature differences. In built-environment applications, such temperature variations are often associated with changes in heat transfer behavior, moisture accumulation, material discontinuities, or subsurface defects, making IRT a valuable diagnostic tool for condition assessment and performance evaluation and for identifying energy inefficiencies and material degradation that impact the sustainability of built systems [ 24 ,  77 ].

In infrastructure and building inspection, UAV-based infrared thermography (UAV-IRT) extends the utility of conventional thermography by enabling rapid, remote, and flexible thermal data acquisition across large, complex, or difficult-to-access assets. Compared with manual inspection or ground-based thermal surveys, UAV-mounted thermal cameras improve accessibility, reduce safety risks, and support efficient inspection of roofs, façades, bridge components, and other elevated or spatially distributed surfaces [ 78 ]. Prior studies have demonstrated the applicability of UAV-IRT for building envelope assessment, heat-loss detection, façade anomaly identification, and thermal transmittance evaluation, highlighting its growing role in building diagnostics and infrastructure inspection workflows and its potential to support energy-efficient building operation and maintenance practices [ 23 ,  39 ,  68 ,  72 ,  111 ].

The effectiveness of UAV-IRT depends not only on thermal sensing itself but also on platform characteristics and sensor deployment strategies. UAV platforms generally include multi-rotor systems, which are well suited for close-range inspection due to their maneuverability and hovering capability, and fixed-wing systems, which are more appropriate for broader-area coverage in linear or large-scale inspections [ 78 ]. In many inspection applications, thermal cameras are integrated with RGB cameras and, in some cases, LiDAR or photogrammetric systems to enable multimodal sensing and improve spatial interpretation of thermal data [ 20 ,  91 ]. The specific UAV–sensor configuration should therefore be selected according to inspection objectives, target geometry, required resolution, and site constraints to ensure both technical accuracy and efficient resource utilization in inspection processes.

Operational and environmental conditions are especially important in UAV-IRT because thermal readings are highly sensitive to data acquisition settings and external influences. Flight altitude, viewing geometry, image overlap, and temporal scheduling affect the spatial resolution and interpretability of collected thermal imagery, while solar radiation, wind speed, ambient temperature, surface emissivity, and thermal inertia can significantly influence measured temperature patterns [ 24 ,  59 ]. In quantitative applications, sensor calibration and environmental compensation become even more critical, particularly when UAV-IRT is used to estimate thermal properties such as heat-transfer performance or U-values [ 72 ,  91 ,  111 ]. These factors explain why data quality, repeatability, and measurement reliability remain central concerns in UAV-based thermal inspection research and are essential for generating reliable data to support sustainable decision-making in infrastructure management.

From a theoretical perspective, UAV-IRT should not be viewed merely as an imaging technology, but as a sensing modality whose value depends on the interaction among thermal physics, sensing geometry, environmental context, and downstream data interpretation. As illustrated in Fig.  1 , UAV-based infrared thermography can be understood as a workflow that links infrared radiation principles, UAV-based thermal sensing, environmental influences, thermal image processing, and defect detection. This is particularly relevant for review studies such as the present one, because the usefulness of UAV-IRT in digital inspection workflows depends not only on defect visibility at the image level, but also on the extent to which thermal data can be processed, spatially aligned, semantically interpreted, and integrated into broader decision-support environments that support efficient, data-driven, and sustainability-oriented infrastructure management practices.

sections.heading: BIM and DTs in infrastructure management
paragraphs: BIM represents a paradigm shift in the AEC/FM industry, moving from traditional 2D drawings to intelligent 3D models that contain rich, structured data. BIM facilitates collaborative workflows, improves project delivery, and supports lifecycle management of assets from design and construction through operation and maintenance [ 65 ,  95 ]. Its evolution has led to a more integrated and data-centric approach to managing built environments, which is essential for improving resource efficiency and supporting sustainable infrastructure development.

The emergence of DTs in infrastructure monitoring further extends the capabilities of BIM by creating a virtual replica of a physical asset, system, or process. Unlike static BIM models, DTs are dynamic virtual representations that are periodically or near-real-time updated with data from physical sensors, enabling monitoring, analysis, and predictive capabilities [ 63 ]. This allows for proactive decision-making, optimized performance, and enhanced asset longevity, which are critical for reducing lifecycle resource consumption and improving the sustainability of infrastructure systems. The key differences between BIM and DTs are summarized in Table  1 .

Table 1 Key Differences between BIM and DTs Feature BIM DTs Nature Structured digital information model Dynamic virtual representation Primary focus Design, construction, and asset information management Monitoring, analysis, and lifecycle optimization Data role Information repository and coordination platform Continuously or near-real-time updated decision-support environment Interoperability function Provides semantic and geometric asset context Integrates sensor streams and operational data Update pattern Periodic or project-based Continuous or near-real-time Typical use Documentation, coordination, facility information Condition monitoring, prediction, maintenance optimization

Although BIM and DTs are frequently discussed together in the literature, they serve different roles within digital inspection ecosystems. BIM primarily functions as a structured information repository and semantic representation of physical assets, providing geometric, material, and asset-level context [ 36 ,  63 ]. In contrast, DTs extend BIM capabilities by incorporating continuously updated sensing data, enabling condition monitoring, performance assessment, anomaly tracking, and predictive maintenance [ 81 ]. Therefore, BIM can be viewed as an important enabling foundation for DT implementation, while DTs represent a higher level of digital maturity characterized by dynamic data integration and closed-loop decision support [ 63 ,  81 ]. Within UAV-IRT workflows, BIM supports defect localization and semantic mapping, whereas DTs support temporal monitoring, model updating, and lifecycle decision-making.

sections.heading: Digital inspection workflows in AEC
paragraphs: Inspection practices in the AEC industry are increasingly shifting from isolated, manual, and document-based procedures toward digital inspection workflows supported by sensing, computation, and model-based integration [ 41 ,  75 ]. This shift reflects broader changes in asset management, where the objective is no longer limited to identifying visible defects, but extends to creating traceable, analyzable, and decision-ready inspection information that can support maintenance planning and lifecycle management, thereby reducing unnecessary interventions and lowering resource use in infrastructure systems. As a result, inspection is becoming a multi-stage digital process rather than a stand-alone field activity.

A typical digital inspection workflow can be conceptualized as a four-stage pipeline consisting of: data acquisition, data processing, asset model integration, and decision support. In the first stage, sensing technologies such as UAVs, RGB cameras, thermal cameras, LiDAR, or other non-contact systems are used to collect raw inspection data. In the second stage, these raw data are processed through operations such as image correction, registration, anomaly detection, classification, and 3D reconstruction. In the third stage, processed inspection outputs are linked to asset models, such as BIM or related digital representations, to provide spatial, semantic, and operational context. Finally, in the fourth stage, integrated information is used to support maintenance prioritization, condition assessment, predictive analytics, and other decision-making tasks ([ 41 ]; [ 61 ,  104 ,  106 ]), which can contribute to more sustainable maintenance strategies and long-term infrastructure resilience. This multi-stage digital transformation process, specifically tailored for UAV-IRT integration within BIM and DT frameworks, is conceptualized and illustrated in Fig.  2 .
Fig. 2 Typical digital inspection pipeline

This pipeline is enabled by the convergence of several technologies. UAV sensing improves access and inspection efficiency; AI-based methods support automated defect detection and interpretation; photogrammetry and other reconstruction methods generate spatially explicit digital representations; BIM provides semantic and asset-level context; and DT frameworks extend these capabilities toward time-dependent monitoring and predictive maintenance [ 41 ,  52 ,  61 ,  93 ,  104 ,  106 ]. Importantly, these components should not be understood as independent tools, but as functionally connected parts of a digital inspection ecosystem, supporting integrated and sustainability-oriented asset management practices.

From a theoretical standpoint, digital inspection workflows represent a transition from data collection to information integration and, ultimately, to actionable intelligence. This perspective is especially important for the present review, because the significance of UAV-IRT lies not only in its sensing capability, but in its position within a larger workflow that transforms thermal observations into model-linked and decision-relevant asset knowledge, enabling more efficient, data-driven, and sustainable infrastructure management decisions.

sections.heading: Positioning UAV-IRT within BIM and DT ecosystems
paragraphs: Within the broader digital inspection landscape, UAV-based infrared thermography occupies a strategically important but still under-integrated position. On one hand, UAV-IRT provides rich thermal diagnostic information that can reveal building envelope anomalies, heat-loss regions, moisture-related effects, and defect signatures that are difficult to identify reliably through visible inspection alone ([ 79 ,  90 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 113 ] b). On the other hand, thermal inspection outputs are still frequently treated as isolated images, orthomosaics, or project-specific analyses, rather than as interoperable data assets that can be linked to digital asset models and maintenance systems [ 79 ,  90 ], limiting their potential to support sustainable asset management and long-term performance optimization.

This disconnect represents a central challenge in current research and practice. Thermal data often lack direct semantic association with asset components, are difficult to spatially register with model geometry, and are not consistently incorporated into maintenance workflows or lifecycle databases [ 7 ,  20 ,  35 ,  71 ,  91 ]. As a result, the practical value of UAV-IRT is often constrained to one-time diagnosis rather than continuous condition monitoring, anomaly tracking, and maintenance decision support. This limitation is particularly significant in complex infrastructure and facility management contexts, where the usefulness of inspection data depends on traceability, spatial context, temporal comparability, and decision relevance, all of which are critical for enabling efficient resource use and sustainable infrastructure management.

Integrating UAV-IRT with BIM and DT environments offers a pathway to overcome these limitations. Although BIM and DTs are often discussed together, they serve different functions within digital inspection ecosystems. In this review, BIM is treated primarily as the semantic integration layer linking UAV-derived thermal information to asset components, whereas DTs are treated as dynamic decision-support environments that utilize BIM-linked inspection information for monitoring, condition assessment, and predictive maintenance. BIM therefore provides the structured asset context necessary for organizing and contextualizing inspection data, while DTs extend this capability through continuous data updating, performance tracking, and lifecycle decision support, thereby representing a higher level of digital maturity and dynamism. Importantly, this distinction enables thermal observations to be incorporated into DT environments at a higher temporal frequency without requiring equivalent updates to the underlying BIM geometry, thereby supporting continuous condition assessment while maintaining a stable asset information model. In practice, this reflects the increasingly adopted view that BIM serves as a relatively stable semantic representation of the asset, whereas DT environments accommodate dynamic inspection and operational data streams [ 36 ,  63 ,  81 ].

First, thermal anomalies can be spatially contextualized by mapping them to corresponding building or infrastructure elements within a three-dimensional digital model, thereby improving localization, interpretation, and reporting ([ 80 ,  93 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 107 ] b). Second, integration enables thermal observations to be linked with semantic information, inspection history, and asset metadata, creating a more structured basis for defect documentation and comparison over time [ 7 ,  56 ,  103 ]. Third, when connected to DT environments, UAV-IRT data can contribute to condition monitoring and predictive maintenance by supporting model updating, anomaly tracking, and performance-based decision-making [ 36 ,  63 ,  81 ,  87 ,  112 ]. In this way, UAV-IRT becomes more than a sensing method; it becomes a data source within a digital asset environment capable of supporting condition assessment, anomaly tracking, predictive maintenance, and lifecycle decision-making.

A typical UAV-IRT integration workflow involves several sequential steps. Following UAV-based thermal image acquisition, thermal datasets are processed through image correction, photogrammetric reconstruction, thermal analysis, and anomaly identification procedures [ 71 ,  81 ]. The resulting thermal information must then be spatially registered and semantically mapped to corresponding BIM elements to establish meaningful associations between detected anomalies and physical asset components [ 35 ,  56 ,  91 ]. Once linked to BIM, inspection information can be incorporated into DT environments together with historical inspection records, sensor measurements, and asset metadata to support condition monitoring, performance assessment, and lifecycle analysis.

Despite recent advances, several technical challenges remain. Accurate registration between thermal imagery and digital models can be difficult due to geometric distortions, varying image resolutions, and environmental influences. Additional challenges include semantic mapping consistency, automated defect-to-component association, interoperability across software platforms, and the integration of heterogeneous data formats into unified BIM- and DT-based asset management systems [ 7 ].

Recent studies have begun to demonstrate elements of this integration through image-to-BIM registration, BIM-enriched thermal mapping, thermography-supported DT workflows, and model-based defect management frameworks ([ 14 ,  36 ,  56 ,  81 ,  87 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 109 , ], Zhang, [ 105 ] a; [ 112 ]). Nevertheless, these efforts remain fragmented, and a fully mature workflow that consistently connects UAV-IRT acquisition, data processing, semantic mapping, and lifecycle decision support has not yet been established. This unresolved integration challenge provides the conceptual basis for the present review, limiting the scalability of sustainability-oriented digital inspection practices.

Accordingly, this review positions UAV-IRT at the intersection of three converging research streams: non-contact thermal inspection, model-based digital representation, and data-driven asset management. These domains are reviewed together because the value of UAV-IRT increasingly depends not only on defect detection itself, but also on the ability to integrate inspection information into BIM-enabled asset representations and DT-enabled monitoring and decision-support environments.

As illustrated in Fig.  3 , UAV-IRT can be conceptually positioned within a hierarchical digital inspection framework that progresses from sensing and data processing to BIM-enabled semantic integration, DT-enabled monitoring and analytics, and ultimately decision-support applications. This framework highlights the fundamental connections among UAV sensing, BIM, and DT technologies and provides the conceptual basis for examining them within a unified review.

Understanding this intersection is essential for identifying not only what UAV-IRT can detect, but also how its outputs can be transformed into scalable, interoperable, and decision-supportive resources within BIM and DT ecosystems, ultimately supporting more sustainable, resilient, and resource-efficient infrastructure systems.

sections.heading: Literature search strategy
paragraphs: To ensure a comprehensive and transparent synthesis of existing research, a structured literature search was conducted across multiple major academic sources covering engineering, construction management, remote sensing, and computer science research. The search was conducted without an explicit lower year limit and covered publications available up to March 2026. Scopus and Web of Science were used as the primary indexing databases, while publisher platforms and digital libraries, including ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, and Wiley Online Library, were used for supplementary searches to improve coverage of relevant journal articles and conference proceedings. Because many publications are indexed in multiple databases, records retrieved from different sources were consolidated prior to screening to remove potential duplicates.

The search strategy was designed to capture studies addressing the intersection of UAV-based sensing, infrared thermography, and digital asset modeling within the context of infrastructure inspection and building performance analysis, with particular attention to applications related to energy performance, resource efficiency, and sustainable infrastructure management. To achieve this objective, a set of keyword combinations and Boolean search operators was developed to identify relevant publications while maintaining sufficient breadth to avoid excluding emerging research topics.
The primary Boolean search strings used in the database queries included the following:

(UAV OR drone OR UAS) AND thermography AND building inspection. (UAV OR drone) AND “thermal imaging” AND building energy. (UAV OR drone) AND thermography AND BIM. (UAV OR drone) AND thermography AND “digital twin”. thermal imaging AND BIM AND building inspection. drone AND thermal imaging AND building envelope.

These search queries were intentionally formulated to capture a wide range of studies spanning multiple research domains, including UAV–enabled inspection technologies, thermal imaging analysis, BIM-based data integration, and DT–supported infrastructure monitoring, as well as studies relevant to improving energy efficiency and supporting sustainability-oriented building and infrastructure practices. This broad search strategy helped ensure that the review encompassed both foundational research and recent advances related to UAV-IRT applications and their integration into digital infrastructure management environments.

The search process focused primarily on peer-reviewed journal articles and conference proceedings, which represent the dominant publication formats in engineering and construction technology research, ensuring the inclusion of high-quality studies relevant to both technical development and sustainability-related applications.

sections.heading: Screening and selection process
paragraphs: The screening process follows a structured and transparent filtering procedure inspired by PRISMA principles and adapted for engineering and construction review studies. Following the literature search, the identified publications were subjected to a multi-stage screening and selection procedure designed to refine the dataset and ensure relevance to the research scope. This process followed a structured filtering procedure commonly adopted in engineering and construction review studies to enhance transparency and reproducibility in literature selection. The initial database search yielded 353 publications. These records were then evaluated through three successive screening stages.

sections.heading: Title screening
paragraphs: In the first stage, article titles were reviewed to remove publications clearly unrelated to the review scope. Studies that did not involve UAV technologies, infrared thermography, building or infrastructure inspection, or digital modeling environments such as BIM or DTs were excluded at this stage.

sections.heading: Abstract screening
paragraphs: In the second stage, the abstracts of the remaining publications were examined to evaluate their relevance to the thematic focus of the review. Articles were retained if they addressed at least one of the following aspects:

UAV-based inspection or sensing technologies. infrared thermography applied to buildings or infrastructure. integration of inspection data with BIM or digital models. DT–based monitoring or asset management in contexts relevant to efficient lifecycle management and sustainability-oriented applications.
Publications that focused on unrelated sensing domains or applications outside the built environment were excluded.

sections.heading: Full-text evaluation
paragraphs: In the final stage, the full texts of the remaining publications were carefully reviewed to confirm their relevance and to extract detailed information regarding methodologies, application contexts, data processing approaches, and integration strategies. Studies were retained if they provided meaningful insights into UAV-based infrared thermography (UAV-IRT), thermal data interpretation, or the integration of inspection data with BIM and DT environments. To be included in the final dataset, studies were required to address at least one of the following aspects: UAV-IRT inspection applications, thermal data processing or anomaly interpretation, BIM-based integration of inspection outputs, or DT–enabled monitoring and asset management, particularly where these contribute to improved resource efficiency and long-term infrastructure performance. The inclusion and exclusion criteria applied throughout the screening process are summarized in Table  2 .

After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria summarized in Table  2  and completing the multi-stage screening process, a final dataset of 110 publications was identified as sufficiently relevant for detailed qualitative synthesis and thematic analysis. The final dataset includes journal articles, conference papers, and a small number of book chapters, covering research related to UAV inspection, thermal imaging, BIM integration, and DT–based infrastructure monitoring, including studies addressing energy performance, maintenance efficiency, and sustainability-related outcomes in built environments. The temporal trend shows that research on UAV-based infrared thermography and its integration with BIM and DT environments has grown substantially in recent years, with a particularly notable increase after 2021. This pattern indicates that the topic has evolved into an active and expanding research area, especially in relation to multimodal sensing, AI-assisted analysis, and digital asset integration, with increasing relevance to sustainability-driven digital transformation in the AEC industry.

sections.heading: Statement on AI assistance in manuscript preparation
paragraphs: During the development of this manuscript, the authors utilized a large language model (Generative Pre-trained Transformer - GPT) specifically for linguistic refinement, proofreading, and improving the grammatical flow of the text. It is important to note that the AI tool was not used to conduct the literature search, perform the screening of the 110 identified publications, or generate the conceptual frameworks (such as the thematic classification in Sect.   3.3 ). All search strategies, data extraction, and synthesis of findings were performed by the human authors, who maintain full responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of the final content.

sections.heading: Literature classification framework
paragraphs: To facilitate structured analysis of the selected literature, a classification framework was developed to organize the identified studies according to their primary research focus. This framework enables comparative analysis across different research directions and helps identify major technological developments, methodological patterns, and remaining research gaps within the field, including those related to improving resource efficiency and supporting sustainable infrastructure management.

Based on thematic analysis of the selected publications, the literature was grouped into four main research categories representing the dominant research streams in UAV-IRT–related infrastructure inspection studies:

UAV-IRT inspection applications – studies focusing on the practical use of UAV-based infrared thermography for defect detection, condition assessment, and infrastructure diagnostics. Thermal data processing and analysis – studies addressing thermal image processing, anomaly detection algorithms, machine learning techniques, and automated interpretation of thermal inspection data. BIM integration approaches – research investigating the registration, mapping, and semantic integration of UAV inspection outputs within BIM environments. DT frameworks – studies exploring dynamic monitoring, model updating, predictive maintenance, and lifecycle asset management using DT systems linked with inspection data, with increasing emphasis on enabling efficient resource use and sustainable asset lifecycle optimization.

This classification framework allows the literature to be analyzed along a progressive technological pipeline, moving from data acquisition and sensing technologies toward digital model integration and decision-support applications. Such a structured categorization also provides the conceptual basis for organizing the thematic discussions presented in the subsequent sections of this review, highlighting how different technological components contribute to more efficient and sustainability-oriented infrastructure management workflows. sections.heading: UAV-IRT applications in infrastructure inspection
paragraphs: Unmanned aerial vehicle–based infrared thermography (UAV-IRT) has emerged as an effective non-contact sensing approach for infrastructure inspection, enabling rapid, non-contact thermal diagnostics across a wide range of built-environment assets [ 78 ]. Compared with conventional inspection approaches that rely on manual surveys or ground-based instruments, UAV-IRT provides improved accessibility, faster data acquisition, and spatially continuous thermal information over large areas [ 26 ,  78 ]. These capabilities have enabled UAV-IRT to support condition assessment, defect detection, and performance evaluation in multiple infrastructure domains, including transportation systems, bridges, and building envelopes ([ 72 ,  77 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 113 ] b; [ 111 ]), thereby supporting more efficient inspection practices and contributing to reduced resource consumption in infrastructure management. In addition to building and transportation infrastructure, UAV-based thermography has also been explored in other inspection contexts such as industrial facilities, heritage structures, and energy systems ([ 6 ,  12 ,  18 ,  57 ,  70 ,  73 ,  74 ,  89 ,  96 ]; S. Zhang et al., [ 114 ]. This section synthesizes representative application areas identified in the reviewed literature and discusses how UAV-IRT contributes to defect detection and infrastructure diagnostics in ways that support sustainable and data-driven asset management practices.

sections.heading: Pavements and road infrastructure
paragraphs: UAV-IRT has been increasingly explored for the inspection of pavements and road infrastructure, where thermal imaging can assist in identifying subsurface defects and pavement distress [ 26 ,  113 ]. Thermal anomalies captured by UAV platforms may indicate the presence of subsurface voids, moisture intrusion, delamination, or material deterioration that are not easily detectable through visual inspection alone. These early-stage defects often represent precursors to more severe structural failures and therefore provide valuable information for preventive maintenance strategies, helping to extend pavement lifespan and reduce material consumption associated with large-scale repairs.

In addition to pavement monitoring, recent studies have also investigated how environmental and climatic conditions influence the thermal detectability of defects in transportation infrastructure, particularly in concrete bridge decks. These studies highlight the importance of considering regional climate zones and environmental conditions when interpreting UAV-based thermographic inspection results [ 2 ,  3 ,  4 ].

The non-contact and mobile nature of UAV platforms enables efficient scanning of large pavement surfaces, including highways and airport runways, with minimal disruption to traffic operations. By analyzing spatial temperature variations across pavement surfaces, inspectors can identify areas exhibiting abnormal heat transfer behavior that may correspond to structural weaknesses or moisture-related damage. Such capabilities have demonstrated potential for improving the efficiency of pavement monitoring and supporting targeted maintenance interventions in transportation infrastructure systems, thereby reducing unnecessary maintenance activities and improving resource efficiency in transportation infrastructure management.

sections.heading: Bridges and structural systems
paragraphs: Bridge inspection represents another important application area for UAV-IRT. Many bridge components, particularly bridge decks and supporting structural elements, are susceptible to deterioration processes such as concrete delamination, cracking, and moisture penetration. Infrared thermography can reveal these defects by detecting localized temperature differences caused by variations in thermal conductivity, material bonding conditions, or internal voids associated with subsurface delamination in concrete bridge decks [ 4 ,  26 ,  76 ].

UAV platforms enable inspectors to access hard-to-reach structural components, including bridge undersides, deck surfaces, and elevated structural members. Thermal imagery collected during UAV flights can be used to generate spatial thermal maps that highlight temperature gradients associated with potential structural anomalies. These thermal patterns can indicate subsurface delamination, debonding, or moisture accumulation within concrete bridge decks, which are critical indicators of structural degradation [ 2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  16 ,  76 ,  113 ].

By facilitating rapid inspection and improved spatial coverage, UAV-IRT supports more proactive bridge maintenance practices and contributes to early defect identification. Such capabilities are particularly valuable for aging bridge networks where frequent monitoring is required to ensure structural safety and serviceability [ 26 ], while also enabling more efficient maintenance planning by facilitating early detection of structural defects, thereby reducing resource-intensive repair interventions over the asset lifecycle.

sections.heading: Buildings and energy diagnostics
paragraphs: Among the various application domains, building inspection and energy diagnostics represent one of the most extensively studied uses of UAV-IRT [ 78 ]. Thermal imaging is widely applied for building envelope inspection, where it can reveal heat loss, insulation deficiencies, air leakage pathways, and moisture-related defects. Because thermal radiation patterns directly reflect heat transfer behavior across building surfaces, UAV-IRT provides an effective means of evaluating building energy performance and identifying envelope failures, thereby reducing building energy losses associated with envelope defects and contributing to improved energy efficiency, which is critical for supporting sustainable building operation.

Numerous studies have demonstrated the capability of UAV-IRT to detect thermal bridges, facade degradation, insulation discontinuities, and air leakage in building envelopes. These defects often result in significant energy losses and reduced thermal comfort if left unaddressed, leading to increased energy consumption and reduced sustainability performance of buildings. UAV-based thermographic surveys allow inspectors to capture comprehensive thermal views of building facades and roof systems, enabling more efficient energy audits compared with traditional handheld thermography approaches ([ 15 ,  37 ,  50 ,  54 ,  77 ]; R. Wang et al., [ 100 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 107 ] b; [ 111 ]). These approaches have also been applied to façade defect inspection, 3D thermal mapping, and building-envelope performance analysis in a range of recent studies [ 5 ,  13 ,  28 ,  31 ,  117 ], demonstrating their potential to support energy-efficient building management and sustainability-oriented retrofit strategies.

In addition to energy auditing, UAV-IRT has also been used to detect facade defects such as material degradation, delamination, or moisture accumulation within wall assemblies. When combined with photogrammetry or 3D reconstruction techniques, UAV-IRT can further support spatial mapping of thermal anomalies across entire building envelopes, enabling improved documentation and diagnosis of envelope performance issues, which can inform targeted interventions that reduce material waste and improve long-term resource efficiency [ 50 ,  80 ].

sections.heading: Limitations of standalone UAV-IRT workflows
paragraphs: Despite the significant advantages offered by UAV-IRT in infrastructure inspection, many existing workflows remain limited by the isolated use of thermal data [ 79 ,  90 ]. In numerous applications, thermal imagery or orthomosaics are analyzed independently from digital asset models or facility management systems. As a result, thermal inspection outputs often remain detached from the semantic and geometric information required for comprehensive infrastructure management, limiting their effectiveness in supporting efficient decision-making.

One key limitation is the difficulty of spatially contextualizing detected thermal anomalies within the broader structure of an infrastructure asset. Without integration with structured digital models such as BIM or DTs, thermal observations cannot be easily linked to specific building components, structural elements, or asset inventories. This limitation reduces the usefulness of UAV-IRT data for maintenance planning and long-term asset management ([ 79 ]; [ 80 ,  90 ]), and constrains their ability to support resource-efficient lifecycle management strategies.

Another challenge involves the lack of automated semantic interpretation of detected anomalies. In many workflows, thermal anomalies are identified visually by inspectors, but they are not automatically translated into meaningful defect categories or severity levels. Consequently, the interpretation process remains heavily dependent on expert judgment and manual analysis, limiting scalability and operational efficiency [ 62 ], which can hinder the broader adoption of efficient and sustainability-driven inspection practices.

Furthermore, standalone UAV-IRT workflows often exhibit limited integration with maintenance planning systems or lifecycle management platforms. Without connection to digital asset models or monitoring systems, thermal inspection results cannot be readily incorporated into predictive maintenance strategies. These limitations highlight the growing need to integrate UAV-IRT data with structured digital environments such as BIM and DTs, where inspection outputs can be linked with asset information, maintenance histories, and operational monitoring systems to support more intelligent and data-driven infrastructure management workflows, ultimately enabling more sustainable, efficient, and resilient infrastructure systems. Accordingly, recent research has increasingly focused on integrating UAV-IRT data with BIM and DT environments to overcome these limitations.

sections.heading: Integrating UAV-IRT with BIM and DTs
paragraphs: The integration of UAV-based infrared thermography with BIM and DT ecosystems represents a critical step toward intelligent infrastructure inspection and asset management. While UAV-IRT enables efficient thermal data acquisition, its full value can only be realized when inspection outputs are integrated with structured digital models that support spatial analysis, data management, and lifecycle decision-making, thereby enabling more efficient use of resources in infrastructure management. Recent studies increasingly emphasize linking UAV-derived thermal data with BIM environments and DT frameworks to enable more comprehensive monitoring, defect localization, and predictive maintenance capabilities ([ 80 ]; [ 81 ,  93 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 113 ] b), which are essential for reducing unnecessary interventions and improving long-term asset performance. This section synthesizes the key stages involved in this integration pipeline, including data acquisition and preprocessing, thermal data analysis, multimodal data fusion, and model integration within BIM and DT environments (Fig.  6 ), with a focus on how these stages contribute to efficient and sustainable infrastructure management workflows.

sections.heading: UAV-IRT data acquisition and pre-processing
paragraphs: The initial stage of integrating UAV-IRT data into BIM and DT workflows involves careful mission planning and data acquisition procedures designed to ensure data quality and spatial accuracy. Flight planning and mission design must consider several parameters, including flight altitude, sensor resolution, image overlap, viewing geometry, and environmental conditions. These factors directly influence the spatial accuracy and reliability of thermal mapping results obtained from UAV surveys ([ 21 ,  24 ,  27 ,  42 ,  101 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 108 ]; X. Zhang et al., [ 115 ], and play an important role in ensuring efficient data collection and minimizing redundant inspection efforts.

Sensor calibration is another essential step in ensuring the reliability of thermal measurements. Thermal cameras must be calibrated to account for factors such as surface emissivity, atmospheric attenuation, and sensor drift, all of which may influence temperature measurements obtained from aerial surveys [ 24 ,  91 ]. Without appropriate calibration procedures, thermal measurements may lead to inaccurate interpretation of structural defects or energy performance conditions, potentially resulting in inefficient maintenance decisions and increased resource use.

Following data acquisition, thermal orthomosaics are typically generated through photogrammetric processing techniques. In this process, individual thermal images are aligned and stitched together to produce a georeferenced thermal map of the inspected infrastructure asset. These orthomosaics provide a spatially continuous representation of surface temperature patterns and enable efficient visualization and analysis of large infrastructure components [ 20 ], supporting more effective identification of defects and reducing the need for repeated inspections.

Additional preprocessing steps are often required to normalize thermal data and reduce environmental influences. Variations in solar radiation, wind speed, and ambient temperature may significantly affect recorded surface temperatures and potentially obscure defect signatures. Data normalization and correction techniques are therefore applied to improve dataset consistency and reliability prior to subsequent analysis or integration into digital modeling environments [ 35 ], thereby improving data quality for downstream decision-making and enabling more reliable and resource-efficient maintenance planning.

sections.heading: Thermal data analysis and AI approaches
paragraphs: Once UAV-IRT data have been acquired and preprocessed, the next stage involves thermal data analysis aimed at identifying potential anomalies or defects. Thermal anomaly detection is typically based on identifying spatial temperature variations that deviate from expected thermal patterns within the inspected structure. Such anomalies may indicate moisture intrusion, insulation deficiencies, delamination, or other performance issues in building envelopes and infrastructure components [ 77 ], which are directly related to energy inefficiencies and long-term sustainability performance of built systems.

Image segmentation techniques are commonly used to isolate regions of interest within thermal imagery, separating anomalous thermal patterns from surrounding background areas. These segmentation procedures enable more precise defect localization and support automated inspection workflows, thereby improving efficiency and reducing the need for resource-intensive manual inspections.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence and computer vision have significantly enhanced UAV-IRT data analysis. Similar trends toward AI-assisted decision support and data interpretation have also been observed in broader construction engineering contexts, where AI tools are increasingly used to support data-driven workflows and improve analytical efficiency [ 64 ,  116 ]. Deep learning techniques including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and other deep learning architectures have been widely applied to thermal imagery for automated anomaly detection and defect classification in building inspection scenarios ([ 8 ,  11 ,  43 ,  45 ,  48 ,  51 ,  60 ,  98 ,  99 ,  101 ,  104 ]; X. Zhang et al., [ 112 ]. These algorithms can learn characteristic thermal signatures associated with different defect types, thereby reducing the need for manual interpretation and enabling scalable inspection workflows. Thermal imagery has also been incorporated into object detection pipelines to improve automated anomaly identification in aerial inspection scenarios [ 32 ,  113 ]. Recent advances in attention-enhanced object detection architectures have further improved the capability of UAV-based inspection systems to identify small and difficult-to-detect defects. For example, Yang and Mat Isa , [ 102 ] proposed YOLOv10-MsA, which integrates a Manhattan Self-Attention mechanism into the YOLOv10 framework to improve defect detection accuracy while maintaining real-time processing performance for UAV imagery [ 102 ]. Similarly, recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of optimized YOLO architectures and multi-stage CNN frameworks for object detection and structural health monitoring in UAV-enabled inspection applications [ 19 ,  25 ]. For instance, UAV-based infrared imagery combined with deep learning techniques has been used to automatically detect and quantify bridge deck delamination, demonstrating the potential of AI-assisted UAV-IRT workflows for large-scale infrastructure inspection [ 2 ,  113 ].

Table  7  provides a comparative synthesis of representative AI approaches used in UAV-IRT thermal data analysis. Overall, the reviewed studies suggest that no single AI architecture consistently outperforms others across all UAV-IRT inspection scenarios. CNN-based models remain widely used because of their maturity and suitability for thermal anomaly classification and segmentation, whereas YOLO-based detectors are increasingly relevant for real-time UAV inspection due to their fast inference capability. Transformer-based architectures and multimodal AI frameworks show potential for improving contextual understanding and feature representation, but they generally require larger datasets, greater computational resources, and more complex implementation workflows.

However, direct numerical comparison of AI model performance across the reviewed studies remains difficult because datasets, defect types, infrastructure materials, sensing conditions, validation environments, and evaluation metrics vary substantially. As a result, robustness and generalizability remain important unresolved issues. In particular, AI models trained on a specific asset type, material system, or defect category may not perform equally well when applied to different infrastructure types, environmental conditions, or thermal acquisition settings. This limitation is especially important for UAV-IRT because thermal signatures are affected not only by defect characteristics, but also by surface emissivity, solar loading, ambient temperature, wind conditions, sensor resolution, and image-registration quality. Therefore, future AI-assisted UAV-IRT studies should place greater emphasis on cross-site validation, cross-material testing, standardized benchmark datasets, and transparent reporting of model performance under different field conditions.

Another emerging direction is the use of edge computing to support near-real-time UAV-IRT analysis during inspection missions. Rather than transmitting all raw thermal imagery to remote servers for post-processing, edge-enabled UAV workflows could perform preliminary anomaly detection, image-quality screening, data filtering, or compression onboard the UAV or through nearby edge devices [ 84 ,  88 ]. This capability could allow inspectors to identify suspicious thermal patterns during flight, adjust flight paths, recapture low-quality images, and reduce unnecessary data transmission. Such functionality is particularly relevant for large infrastructure assets where inspection efficiency and timely feedback are important. However, edge-enabled UAV-IRT also introduces challenges related to onboard computational capacity, battery consumption, payload constraints, model compression, thermal-image reliability, and the need for lightweight yet accurate AI models. Therefore, edge computing should be viewed as a promising but still emerging pathway for improving the operational efficiency and responsiveness of UAV-IRT inspection workflows. AI-driven analysis frameworks also enable automated defect classification and prioritization. Detected anomalies can be categorized according to defect type, severity, and potential structural implications. Deep learning models have also been applied to identify thermal anomalies related to moisture infiltration and seepage in infrastructure systems [ 46 ,  62 ]. Such automated interpretation supports faster inspection workflows and improves consistency in defect assessment, thereby enabling more efficient maintenance planning.

sections.heading: Multimodal data fusion and 3D reconstruction
paragraphs: To enhance defect interpretation and spatial understanding of inspection results, many recent studies employ multimodal data fusion strategies. These approaches combine thermal imagery with additional sensing modalities such as RGB imagery and LiDAR point clouds to produce more informative datasets for infrastructure inspection ([ 10 ,  21 ,  22 ,  27 ,  40 ,  53 ,  90 ,  101 ]; X. Zhang et al., [ 112 ], enabling more comprehensive condition assessment and reducing uncertainty in inspection outcomes.

RGB imagery provides high-resolution visual information and geometric context, while thermal imagery captures temperature distribution and heat transfer behavior across infrastructure surfaces. LiDAR data contribute highly accurate geometric measurements that enable precise spatial modeling of infrastructure components.

Photogrammetry techniques are widely used to generate detailed three-dimensional models from overlapping UAV imagery, enabling the spatial integration of thermal and geometric datasets in building and infrastructure inspection workflows [ 1 ,  11 ,  17 ,  20 ,  34 ,  43 ,  48 ,  67 ,  92 ,  98 ]. The transition from raw thermal images to thermal point clouds or textured meshes generally requires several processing steps. First, thermal images are corrected and calibrated to improve radiometric consistency and reduce sensor- or acquisition-related distortion. Second, overlapping UAV images are aligned through photogrammetric reconstruction procedures, such as structure-from-motion and multi-view stereo workflows, often supported by RGB imagery because thermal images typically have lower spatial resolution and fewer stable visual features for image matching. Third, thermal and RGB datasets are co-registered using camera calibration parameters, shared control points, image features, or estimated camera poses so that temperature values can be accurately associated with reconstructed geometry. Finally, thermal information can be projected onto three-dimensional meshes as thermal textures or converted into thermal point clouds, followed by georeferencing or coordinate transformation to support integration with BIM and DT environments. This process is technically demanding because calibration errors, weak thermal features, resolution differences between RGB and thermal imagery, and registration inaccuracies can directly affect the reliability of defect localization and subsequent asset-level interpretation. For example, recent studies have demonstrated that fusing UAV-based thermal imagery with visible photogrammetric data can generate high-resolution thermal point clouds for building roof inspection and energy performance analysis [ 21 ], supporting more accurate identification of energy-related deficiencies and performance issues.

Several workflow-oriented studies have proposed integrated drone-based survey pipelines that combine photogrammetry and thermography to improve the spatial mapping of building defects and energy anomalies [ 71 ]. For example, time-lapse drone thermography has been used to generate thermal orthomosaics and point clouds that support building envelope anomaly characterization and integration with building energy modeling environments [ 77 ]. These integrated workflows enable thermal inspection results to be spatially aligned with three-dimensional models, thereby supporting more accurate defect localization and infrastructure condition assessment, which can inform targeted interventions that reduce material waste and improve lifecycle efficiency.

Thermal texture mapping is commonly applied to project thermal data onto reconstructed 3D models. This process creates thermal-textured models in which temperature information is directly associated with the geometry of the inspected asset. Such models provide improved spatial context for identifying and interpreting thermal anomalies within infrastructure components ([ 10 ,  90 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 113 ] b), enhancing decision-making accuracy and reducing the likelihood of unnecessary maintenance actions.

Advanced reconstruction workflows may further combine photogrammetry and LiDAR datasets to produce accurate multimodal models suitable for integration with BIM and DT platforms. The fusion of geometric and thermal information significantly enhances the interpretability of inspection results and supports more informed infrastructure assessment and management decisions [ 10 ,  20 ,  90 ], thereby contributing to more efficient, data-driven, and sustainable infrastructure management practices.

sections.heading: Integration into BIM and DT platforms
paragraphs: While Sect.   5.3  focuses on multimodal sensing and 3D reconstruction processes, the ultimate objective of UAV-IRT data processing is the integration of inspection results into BIM and DT environments. Through this integration, raw inspection data can be transformed into structured information that supports asset management and infrastructure monitoring workflows, thereby enabling more efficient decision-making by linking inspection results with asset information and reducing unnecessary maintenance interventions.

One key step in this process is the mapping of detected thermal anomalies to BIM elements. By associating thermal observations with specific building components such as walls, roofs, structural members, or façade elements, inspection results can be spatially contextualized within a digital building model ([ 80 ,  93 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 113 ] b). This mapping process enables precise localization of defects and facilitates targeted maintenance planning by enabling early identification of affected components and reducing unnecessary interventions.

The integration of thermal inspection data also enables semantic enrichment of BIM models. Thermal anomalies can be linked with additional metadata, including material properties, construction details, inspection records, and maintenance history. Such enriched datasets improve the interpretability of inspection findings and support more informed infrastructure management decisions by enabling more accurate assessment of defect severity and prioritization of maintenance actions [ 62 ].

Within DT frameworks, BIM models enriched with inspection data can be dynamically updated to reflect the current condition of the physical infrastructure asset. DT environments allow inspection results to be continuously incorporated into a virtual representation of the infrastructure system, enabling ongoing condition monitoring and performance evaluation [ 63 ]. Recent research has also explored advanced neural rendering techniques, such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), to enhance DT representations and improve the integration of multimodal sensing data within dynamic infrastructure models [ 36 ], thereby enabling more accurate tracking of asset condition changes over time and supporting timely maintenance decisions.

Ultimately, integrating UAV-IRT data with BIM and DT platforms supports more advanced asset management strategies by establishing a clearer pathway from thermal observation to maintenance decision-making. In this pathway, (1) thermal anomalies are first detected from UAV-IRT data and screened with attention to uncertainty caused by acquisition conditions, environmental effects, and sensor limitations; (2) confirmed or suspected anomalies are spatially registered and mapped to corresponding BIM elements or asset components; (3) these records are enriched with metadata such as inspection date, sensor settings, environmental conditions, material type, component location, and maintenance history; (4) the integrated information is interpreted in terms of defect severity, asset criticality, recurrence, and potential performance impact; and (5) the resulting component-level information supports maintenance prioritization, repair planning, inspection scheduling, and feedback into DT-based monitoring systems. Through continuous monitoring and model updating, stakeholders can identify emerging issues earlier and support predictive maintenance by reducing large-scale corrective interventions [ 63 ]. In this way, UAV-IRT outputs can move beyond isolated thermal images and become traceable, model-linked, and decision-relevant information for lifecycle asset management.

Beyond technical performance, the integration of UAV-IRT with BIM and DT systems also has important environmental and economic implications. By enabling non-contact inspection and reducing reliance on manual access methods such as scaffolding or rope-based inspection, UAV-IRT may reduce equipment requirements, field operations, and associated resource consumption during inspection activities [ 90 ]. In addition, the ability to detect defects at an early stage supports predictive maintenance strategies, which reduce large-scale repair interventions, minimize material waste, and improve lifecycle resource efficiency [ 63 ,  80 ,  81 ]. Furthermore, integrating thermal inspection data with BIM and DT environments improves maintenance planning, supports more informed decision-making, and reduces unnecessary inspection cycles, contributing to more efficient allocation of labor, time, and financial resources throughout the asset lifecycle [ 63 ,  80 ,  81 ].

sections.heading: Critical evaluation and research synthesis
paragraphs: This section provides a critical synthesis of the reviewed studies by comparing major UAV-IRT integration approaches, evaluating differences in validation and deployment maturity, and identifying cross-cutting trends across literature. Rather than summarizing studies individually, the section synthesizes the reviewed work across levels of digital integration, from standalone UAV-IRT inspection to BIM- and DT-enabled asset management workflows.
