This evidence highlights that the path toward fully mature infrastructure inspection requires harmonizing robust field-validated platforms with generalizable processing and multimodal digital integration workflows.

sections.heading: Validation and research maturity
paragraphs: The reviewed studies also vary considerably in their validation approaches. Many standalone UAV-IRT and AI-assisted studies have been evaluated through field inspections and comparisons with established inspection methods, whereas BIM- and DT-enabled studies are more frequently reported as pilot implementations, prototype workflows, or proof-of-concept demonstrations [ 20 ,  36 ,  56 ,  63 ].

As a result, although the feasibility of BIM- and DT-based integration has been increasingly demonstrated, current evidence remains concentrated on pilot-scale implementations and proof-of-concept applications rather than long-term operational deployment [ 80 ,  81 ]. Consequently, the operational readiness of these approaches has not yet reached the level of more established standalone UAV-IRT inspection workflows, highlighting a need for larger-scale validation and real-world deployment studies.

In addition, the methodological rigor of validation also differs across the reviewed UAV-IRT literature. While some studies compare thermal inspection results against established ground-truth methods such as visual inspection, hammer sounding, impact echo, or in-situ measurements [ 11 ], others primarily demonstrate technical feasibility without extensive quantitative validation [ 36 ,  63 ,  81 ]. Consequently, the reported performance and maturity of UAV-IRT approaches should be interpreted in the context of their underlying validation methodologies [ 11 ,  43 ,  99 ].

sections.heading: Cross-cutting research trends
paragraphs: Across the reviewed studies, a clear maturity gradient is evident across different levels of UAV-IRT research. Sensing technologies, thermal anomaly detection, and AI-assisted analysis have achieved comparatively high levels of technical maturity and validation. In contrast, BIM- and DT-enabled approaches remain constrained by challenges related to interoperability, semantic mapping, workflow automation, lifecycle data management, and the practical implementation of scalable integration frameworks [ 7 ,  80 ,  81 ]. Consequently, the major research bottleneck is no longer the acquisition of thermal information itself, but the ability to consistently transfer, update, and integrate inspection outputs within operational digital asset management environments. This recurring pattern suggests that future advances will depend increasingly on interoperability, workflow automation, and lifecycle information management rather than sensing technologies alone.

Another important cross-cutting observation is that a substantial proportion of the reviewed UAV-IRT literature focuses on concrete-based infrastructure systems, including bridge decks, pavements, and reinforced concrete components [ 98 ]. While many AI-assisted thermal anomaly detection approaches have demonstrated promising performance in these applications, their transferability across other material systems remains insufficiently validated. Thermal signatures are influenced by material-specific properties such as thermal conductivity, heat capacity, emissivity, and moisture behavior, which can vary considerably among concrete, steel, masonry, and composite structures. As a result, defect manifestations and thermal anomaly characteristics may differ across material systems, affecting the transferability of AI-assisted detection approaches [ 33 ,  94 ]. Consequently, AI models and thermal interpretation frameworks developed for one material class may not necessarily achieve comparable performance when applied to different infrastructure systems without additional calibration, retraining, or validation [ 33 ,  94 ]. This limitation highlights the need for broader cross-material validation and more generalized AI-assisted inspection frameworks in future research.

sections.heading: Challenges and research gaps
paragraphs: Despite significant progress achieved in UAV-based infrared thermography and its integration with BIM and DT environments, several technical, analytical, and organizational challenges remain. These challenges limit the large-scale deployment of integrated UAV-IRT inspection workflows in practical infrastructure management scenarios, and constrain their potential to support efficient infrastructure management practices. Addressing these limitations is essential for enabling more reliable, scalable, and automated inspection systems in the built environment, as well as for improving long-term infrastructure performance.

sections.heading: Technical challenges
paragraphs: Technical challenges primarily arise from the limitations of current sensing technologies and the complexity of collecting reliable thermal data under real-world environmental conditions. One key limitation relates to sensor resolution and measurement accuracy. Although UAV-mounted thermal cameras have improved significantly in recent years, their spatial resolution is often lower than that of conventional RGB sensors, which can restrict the detection of small or subtle defects in infrastructure systems [ 78 ,  90 ]. Achieving high spatial resolution while maintaining accurate temperature measurements remains a challenge, particularly when inspecting large structures from aerial platforms, which may lead to missed early-stage defects and reduced efficiency in preventive maintenance strategies [ 78 ]. Previous review studies have similarly noted that defect detectability depends on the interaction among sensor characteristics, acquisition conditions, and target defect properties, making universally applicable hardware selection benchmarks difficult to establish across different infrastructure inspection scenarios. In addition, sensor selection should be aligned with inspection objectives and target defect characteristics, as smaller defects generally require higher spatial resolution, while quantitative thermographic assessments benefit from improved thermal sensitivity and measurement accuracy [ 33 ,  94 ].

Flight operations themselves also impose practical constraints on UAV-IRT deployment. Factors such as limited battery endurance, flight range restrictions, regulatory requirements, line-of-sight operation rules, and site accessibility can affect inspection planning and coverage, particularly for large-scale infrastructure systems [ 26 ,  78 ]. These operational constraints may increase inspection complexity and should be considered when evaluating the practical applicability of UAV-based thermographic inspection workflows [ 62 ].

Environmental influences also introduce substantial uncertainty in thermal data acquisition. Surface temperatures measured through infrared thermography can be significantly affected by solar radiation, wind conditions, humidity, and ambient temperature variations [ 24 ]. Solar radiation plays a critical role in generating thermal contrasts that enable defect detection in many UAV-IRT applications [ 4 ,  16 ]. However, variations in solar loading associated with acquisition timing, surface orientation, shading conditions, and weather fluctuations can significantly influence observed temperature distributions and affect the consistency of thermal interpretation [ 59 ]. Wind conditions can accelerate convective heat transfer and reduce thermal contrasts between defective and non-defective regions, making thermal anomalies more difficult to identify under certain conditions [ 33 ,  94 ]. Thermal measurements may also be influenced by variations in surface emissivity associated with different materials, surface conditions, coatings, and moisture content, which can alter the apparent temperatures recorded by infrared sensors and introduce additional uncertainty into defect interpretation [ 24 ]. Differences in emissivity may cause similar surfaces to exhibit different apparent temperatures even when their actual temperatures are comparable, potentially leading to misinterpretation of thermal signatures if emissivity effects are not properly considered. These observations are consistent with previous review studies identifying environmental conditions, surface properties, and sensor performance as major factors affecting the reliability and detectability of infrared-based defect assessment [ 33 ,  94 ].

As a result, thermal inspections may occasionally produce false-positive indications, while subtle, deeply embedded, or thermally inactive defects may remain undetected, resulting in missed defects or false-negative assessments ([ 33 ]; [ 94 ]). In addition, adverse weather conditions such as strong winds and precipitation may reduce flight stability and further affect the quality and consistency of acquired thermal data (Y. Ma et al., [ 54 ]. Consequently, reliable thermal inspection requires careful mission planning, controlled acquisition conditions, and robust correction algorithms, as well as careful interpretation of thermal signatures to reduce uncertainty in defect assessment [ 71 ,  81 ]. These measures are essential for ensuring accurate decision-making and avoiding inefficient or unnecessary maintenance actions [ 61 ].

Another technical challenge involves calibration consistency across different UAV-IRT systems. Variations in sensor calibration, radiometric correction procedures and atmospheric compensation methods can affect the comparability of thermal measurements obtained from different inspection campaigns or equipment configurations [ 92 ]. In addition, inconsistencies in assumed emissivity values during temperature calibration and data processing may introduce systematic measurement errors across datasets [ 58 ]. Ensuring consistent calibration procedures and standardized acquisition protocols remains essential for achieving reliable quantitative thermography results [ 72 ], particularly for supporting large-scale, data-driven, and resource-efficient infrastructure management workflows. Poor calibration consistency may also reduce the reliability of comparisons across different inspection campaigns, limiting the effectiveness of long-term condition monitoring and trend analysis [ 7 ,  92 ].

sections.heading: Data integration challenges
paragraphs: Another important challenge relates to standards, data formats, and interoperability across UAV-IRT, BIM, and DT environments. While BIM platforms commonly rely on interoperability standards such as Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) to exchange geometric and asset information, thermal imagery, thermal point clouds, orthomosaics, and sensor-derived condition data are often generated and stored in heterogeneous formats ([ 7 ]; [ 80 ,  81 ]). As a result, transferring thermal inspection information between UAV processing software, BIM platforms, and DT environments frequently requires custom workflows, manual data conversion, or project-specific integration solutions. These interoperability limitations can reduce data consistency, hinder automation, and constrain the scalability of UAV-IRT-enabled asset management systems. Future research should focus on developing standardized data structures, interoperable workflows, and open integration frameworks that facilitate seamless information exchange across digital inspection and asset management platforms.

Beyond sensing limitations, significant challenges also arise when integrating UAV-IRT datasets into BIM and DT environments. One major issue involves interoperability between UAV-derived datasets and BIM models. Differences in software platforms, data formats, and coordinate systems can complicate the integration of thermal inspection outputs into existing digital models, often requiring manual processing or customized workflows [ 52 ,  106 ], which reduces scalability and limits the efficiency of digital inspection systems.

Another related challenge concerns the lack of standardized metadata for thermal inspection datasets. Information such as emissivity parameters, environmental conditions, sensor calibration settings, and flight acquisition parameters is frequently inconsistently recorded across studies. This lack of standardized metadata can hinder reliable interpretation and reuse of thermal inspection datasets in BIM-based asset management systems [ 58 ], thereby limiting the potential for consistent, data-driven, and sustainability-oriented decision-making across infrastructure lifecycles.

Long-term data archiving and version control represent additional challenges for UAV-IRT-enabled DT implementation. For thermal inspection data to support multi-year condition monitoring, raw thermal images, processed orthomosaics, thermal point clouds, textured meshes, anomaly labels, and BIM-linked component records must be stored in a traceable and retrievable manner. Each inspection dataset should ideally be associated with inspection date and time, sensor calibration settings, environmental conditions, coordinate reference information, processing workflow version, and linked asset or component identifiers. Without such data governance, it becomes difficult to compare thermal inspection results across time, reproduce prior analyses, or distinguish actual deterioration from changes caused by sensor settings, environmental variability, or data-processing procedures. This issue is particularly important for DT environments, where long-term value depends on maintaining reliable links among historical inspection records, model versions, and decision-support outputs [ 63 ,  83 ].

Model updating also presents a significant challenge for DT environments. DTs are intended to provide continuously updated virtual representations of physical assets, yet incorporating new inspection data into these models remains computationally and methodologically complex. Efficiently updating DTs with UAV-IRT datasets while maintaining model consistency and accuracy continues to be an important research topic [ 63 ], particularly for enabling real-time monitoring and sustainable lifecycle management of infrastructure systems.

sections.heading: Analytical challenges
paragraphs: Analytical challenges are largely related to the interpretation and automated analysis of thermal data, particularly with the increasing use of artificial intelligence techniques. One key limitation is the lack of sufficiently large and well-labeled ground truth datasets for thermal anomaly detection. Developing reliable training datasets that contain accurately annotated defect examples is both time-consuming and resource intensive [ 62 ], which can limit the scalability of AI-driven inspection systems and their potential to support efficient, large-scale infrastructure monitoring.

As a consequence, AI models trained on limited datasets may exhibit poor generalization when applied to different infrastructure types or environmental conditions. Models that perform well in controlled experimental settings may struggle when applied to complex real-world inspection scenarios, where environmental variability and structural diversity introduce additional uncertainty [ 8 ,  11 ,  32 ,  43 ,  45 ,  46 ,  48 ,  62 ,  98 ,  99 ], potentially leading to inaccurate assessments and inefficient allocation of maintenance resources.

Furthermore, many proposed AI-based defect detection methods have been evaluated only through small-scale experiments or limited case studies. The lack of large-scale validation across diverse infrastructure systems restricts the practical applicability of these methods and highlights the need for broader experimental validation and benchmarking in real inspection environments, particularly for enabling reliable, data-driven, and sustainability-oriented infrastructure management practices.

sections.heading: Organizational barriers
paragraphs: In addition to technical and analytical challenges, several organizational barriers also hinder the widespread adoption of integrated UAV-IRT inspection workflows in the AEC/FM industry. One major barrier is the cost associated with deploying advanced sensing technologies, including UAV platforms, thermal imaging sensors, specialized processing software, and data management infrastructure. For many organizations, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, these investments may present significant financial obstacles [ 75 ], which can limit the adoption of efficient and sustainability-enhancing inspection technologies.

The economic value of UAV-IRT should therefore be understood as a context-dependent trade-off rather than as a universally lower-cost alternative to conventional inspection. Compared with scaffolding, lifts, or rope-access methods, UAV-IRT can reduce access-equipment requirements, mobilization time, worker exposure, and disruption to traffic or building operations, particularly for large, elevated, difficult-to-access, or repeatedly inspected assets [ 26 ,  78 ,  86 ]. However, these benefits must be weighed against the costs of UAV platforms, thermal sensors, pilot training, regulatory compliance, specialized software, data processing, calibration, and long-term data management. As a result, UAV-IRT is likely to provide the strongest economic justification in high-risk, large-scale, recurrent, or access-constrained inspection scenarios, whereas its cost-effectiveness may be less evident for small, simple, or one-time inspection tasks. More empirical cost-benefit studies are still needed to quantify these trade-offs across different infrastructure types and operational contexts.

Another important challenge is the shortage of technical expertise required to operate UAV inspection systems and process thermographic datasets in digital inspection workflows [ 9 ,  29 ,  38 ,  47 ,  49 ,  66 ,  69 ,  75 ,  82 ,  97 ]. Successful implementation of UAV-IRT workflows often requires interdisciplinary expertise in remote sensing, thermography, photogrammetry, and BIM technologies, which may not yet be widely available within the construction and facility management workforce [ 75 ], thereby slowing the transition toward more digitalized and sustainability-oriented asset management practices.

Finally, the lack of standardized industry guidelines for UAV-IRT inspection procedures and data integration workflows presents an additional barrier. Without widely accepted standards for data acquisition, processing, and model integration, organizations often adopt fragmented or inconsistent approaches when implementing these technologies. Establishing clearer methodological guidelines and industry standards will therefore be essential for supporting broader adoption of UAV-IRT-enabled digital inspection systems [ 75 ] and for enabling scalable, consistent, and sustainability-driven implementation across the AEC industry.

Legal, regulatory, and privacy considerations also represent important practical barriers to the deployment of thermal-equipped UAVs, particularly in dense urban areas or occupied building environments. In addition to aviation rules, site-specific flight permissions, and operational safety requirements, UAV-IRT inspections may raise privacy concerns because thermal imagery can incidentally capture information from adjacent properties, occupied spaces, or human activity patterns. Although infrastructure inspection does not typically aim to collect personal information, organizations should consider data minimization, secure data storage, access control, retention policies, and clear communication with affected stakeholders. These governance practices are important for maintaining public trust and ensuring that UAV-based inspection workflows remain aligned with broader legal, ethical, and privacy expectations for civil UAV applications [ 30 ,  85 ].

sections.heading: Future research roadmap
paragraphs: Building upon the challenges and research gaps identified in the previous section, this section outlines a future research roadmap aimed at advancing the integration of UAV-based infrared thermography with BIM and DT ecosystems. Existing studies have demonstrated promising progress in UAV-enabled inspection, thermal data processing, and BIM-based integration workflows ([ 80 ,  81 ,  93 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 113 ] b). However, further research is required to develop more scalable, standardized, and intelligent inspection systems capable of supporting infrastructure monitoring and lifecycle management in complex built environments, particularly in ways that improve resource efficiency and support sustainability-oriented asset management practices. Ultimately, the convergence of UAV sensing, AI-driven analytics, and DT platforms may enable the development of autonomous infrastructure inspection ecosystems, where sensing, diagnosis, and maintenance decision-making are increasingly automated, leading to more efficient, resilient, and sustainable infrastructure systems.

To make the roadmap more actionable, the future research directions can be prioritized into near-term needs and longer-term opportunities. In the near term, research should focus on issues that directly affect reliability, reproducibility, and implementation readiness, including standardized UAV-IRT acquisition protocols, consistent thermal metadata, benchmark datasets with ground-truth validation, interoperable BIM/DT data exchange workflows, and explainable AI methods for engineering decision support. In the longer term, research can move toward more advanced capabilities, including multimodal sensing ecosystems, edge-enabled real-time inspection, autonomous UAV monitoring, scalable DT platforms, and predictive maintenance across infrastructure networks. This prioritization suggests that reliable data acquisition, validation, and interoperability should be addressed first, because they provide the foundation for more advanced DT-enabled monitoring and lifecycle asset management.

sections.heading: Workflow standardization
paragraphs: One important research direction involves the development of standardized workflows for integrating UAV-IRT datasets with BIM and DT environments. Current studies often employ customized processing pipelines, resulting in fragmented workflows and limited interoperability between different platforms and software environments. For example, UAV–BIM integration studies have proposed conceptual frameworks and automated inspection workflows, but these approaches remain largely project-specific and lack standardized implementation guidelines ([ 93 ]; [ 106 ]), which limits scalability and reduces the efficiency of digital inspection processes.

Future research should therefore focus on establishing standardized pipelines that connect UAV data acquisition, thermal data processing, and BIM-based model integration. Standardization efforts may include defining recommended flight acquisition parameters, developing consistent thermal data preprocessing procedures, and establishing interoperable data exchange formats that enable seamless communication between UAV platforms, photogrammetric software, BIM systems, and DT platforms. Such efforts would significantly reduce manual processing requirements and improve the reliability and reproducibility of UAV-enabled inspection workflows, while also supporting more efficient use of resources and enabling broader adoption of sustainability-oriented digital inspection practices.

For example, future studies may develop standardized semantic mapping schemas and interoperable data exchange protocols to enable seamless integration between UAV platforms, BIM systems, and DT environments. In addition, current workflows still often lack automated mapping protocols between UAV-derived thermal data (e.g., temperature matrices or thermal images) and BIM elements defined in IFC standards, which limits semantic alignment and seamless interoperability across digital inspection workflows. This limitation also constrains the automated updating of sustainability-related indicators such as energy performance and carbon emissions in BIM- and DT-based asset management systems.

sections.heading: Multimodal sensing integration
paragraphs: Another important research direction involves the integration of UAV-based thermography with additional sensing modalities to enhance infrastructure inspection capabilities. Several studies have explored the combination of thermal imagery with RGB imagery, photogrammetric models, and LiDAR-based datasets to improve the spatial interpretation of inspection results [ 10 ,  20 ,  90 ]. More recent research has further investigated multimodal reconstruction techniques that fuse thermal imagery with RGB and LiDAR data to generate thermally enriched three-dimensional models of infrastructure assets, enabling improved defect localization and spatial analysis ([ 1 ,  17 ,  21 ,  22 ,  27 ,  34 ,  40 ,  48 ,  53 ,  67 ,  92 ,  98 ,  101 ]; X. Zhang et al., [ 112 ], supporting more comprehensive and accurate assessment of infrastructure condition.

Multimodal sensing approaches allow complementary information to be extracted from different sensor types. RGB imagery provides high-resolution visual information and geometric context, while thermal imagery captures temperature distributions associated with heat transfer behavior and potential structural anomalies. LiDAR datasets contribute highly accurate geometric measurements that support precise spatial modeling of infrastructure components and facilitate the registration of inspection datasets.

Future research should focus on developing more advanced data fusion algorithms capable of integrating these heterogeneous datasets into unified digital models. Improved fusion strategies could significantly enhance defect localization accuracy, support more reliable condition assessment, and enable more comprehensive infrastructure monitoring workflows, thereby reducing uncertainty in inspection outcomes and improving the efficiency of maintenance planning and resource allocation. For example, integrated pipelines could be developed to automatically fuse thermal, RGB, and LiDAR data into unified 3D models for infrastructure inspection and defect localization.

sections.heading: AI-enabled decision support
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence represents another critical research direction for advancing UAV-IRT-enabled infrastructure inspection. While recent studies have demonstrated the use of machine learning and deep learning techniques for thermal anomaly detection and automated defect classification [ 60 ,  62 ,  104 ], current approaches remain largely focused on defect detection rather than decision support.

Future research should extend AI applications beyond anomaly detection toward predictive maintenance and infrastructure management applications. Machine learning models could be developed to predict defect progression based on historical inspection datasets and thermal anomaly patterns. Recent studies have applied AI-based thermal image analysis for defect detection and infrastructure condition assessment [ 11 ,  43 ,  48 ,  98 ], suggesting the potential to extend these approaches toward predictive maintenance and deterioration modeling [ 8 ,  32 ,  45 ,  46 ,  51 ,  99 ]. For instance, predictive models that integrate historical thermal inspection data with environmental conditions could help estimate deterioration trends and infrastructure risk over time. Such predictive models could help infrastructure managers prioritize maintenance interventions and allocate resources more efficiently, thereby reducing unnecessary maintenance actions and improving lifecycle resource efficiency.

In addition, integrating AI outputs with BIM and DT platforms could enable more advanced decision-support systems that assist engineers in evaluating infrastructure risk, planning maintenance schedules, and optimizing lifecycle performance. However, the practical adoption of AI-enabled decision-support systems may be constrained by the limited interpretability of some advanced machine learning and deep learning models. Because infrastructure managers and engineers are often required to justify maintenance decisions and allocate substantial resources based on inspection results, explainability, transparency, and user trust remain important considerations for operational deployment. Future research should therefore investigate explainable AI (XAI) approaches capable of providing interpretable insights and supporting engineering judgment alongside automated predictions. These developments can facilitate more efficient resource allocation and risk-informed decision-making in infrastructure asset management, ultimately supporting more sustainable, resilient, and data-driven infrastructure systems. Future studies should also evaluate the robustness and transferability of AI-enabled inspection frameworks across diverse material systems, including steel, masonry, and composite infrastructure, to improve the generalizability of UAV-IRT-based decision-support applications.

sections.heading: Scalable DT ecosystems
paragraphs: Most current DT implementations in infrastructure inspection focus on individual assets or localized case studies. However, the long-term potential of DT technologies lies in their ability to support interconnected infrastructure monitoring systems across larger spatial scales. Several studies have highlighted the importance of DT frameworks for infrastructure monitoring and lifecycle management [ 63 ], particularly in enabling data-driven and system-level decision-making across infrastructure networks.

Future research should therefore explore the development of scalable DT ecosystems capable of integrating inspection data from multiple infrastructure assets within a unified monitoring framework. Such systems could enable coordinated monitoring of buildings, bridges, and transportation infrastructure across urban environments, supporting more efficient management of infrastructure systems at the city scale.

Achieving this vision will require advances in large-scale data management, interoperability between heterogeneous digital models, and visualization tools capable of supporting complex infrastructure systems. These developments would support broader smart city initiatives and enable more proactive infrastructure resilience strategies, while also improving resource efficiency and reducing lifecycle costs across interconnected infrastructure systems. For example, future research may focus on developing cloud-based DT platforms capable of integrating multi-asset inspection data across urban infrastructure systems in real time.

sections.heading: Workforce and education development
paragraphs: Beyond technical advancements, workforce development will play a critical role in enabling the practical adoption of UAV-IRT-enabled inspection systems. The transition from traditional manual inspection to digital, UAV-centric workflows requires several specific skill sets: (1) UAV operation and safety competencies, including flight planning, site risk assessment, regulatory compliance, line-of-sight operation, and mission documentation; (2) thermography-specific competencies, including emissivity selection, sensor calibration, environmental compensation, thermal contrast interpretation, and recognition of possible false positives or missed defects; (3) digital integration competencies, including photogrammetric reconstruction, RGB–thermal registration, thermal point-cloud or mesh generation, BIM element mapping, metadata management, and DT model updating; and (4) data analytics and decision-support competencies, including AI-output interpretation, uncertainty assessment, visualization of inspection results, and translation of thermal anomalies into maintenance priorities. However, the current AEC/FM workforce often lacks interdisciplinary training that integrates these skill sets [ 75 ], which may slow the adoption of efficient and sustainability-oriented digital inspection practices.

Future research should therefore investigate educational frameworks and professional training programs that prepare engineers and technicians to work across both field inspection and digital asset management environments. Such training should combine UAV flight exercises, thermography calibration and interpretation, photogrammetric processing, BIM/DT integration, data-governance practices, and AI-assisted decision-support case studies. Rather than treating UAV operation as a stand-alone technical skill, future curricula and certification programs should emphasize the full inspection-to-decision workflow, from data acquisition and quality control to model integration, anomaly interpretation, and maintenance planning.

Strengthening workforce capabilities will be essential for enabling broader adoption of UAV-IRT-based inspection systems and for supporting the transition toward more intelligent and sustainable infrastructure management practices. These educational and technological priorities collectively form the future research roadmap summarized in Fig.  7 , highlighting the importance of aligning technological innovation with workforce readiness to achieve scalable and sustainable infrastructure systems. For example, interdisciplinary training programs and simulation-based learning environments could be developed to train engineers in UAV operation, thermography, BIM, and AI-enabled inspection workflows.

Collectively, these research directions point toward an integrated and sustainability-oriented digital inspection workflow in which UAV-based sensing, multimodal data fusion, BIM/DT integration, and AI-enabled decision support are seamlessly connected to enable efficient, predictive, and resource-aware infrastructure management.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study presented a structured review of the integration of how UAV-based infrared thermography can be integrated with BIM and DT workflows to support infrastructure inspection, monitoring, and management. The reviewed literature demonstrates that UAV-IRT has significantly expanded the scope and efficiency of infrastructure inspection by enabling rapid, non-contact thermal diagnostics across diverse built-environment assets, including transportation infrastructure, bridges, and building envelopes ([ 26 ,  77 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 113 ] b). Compared with traditional inspection approaches, UAV-IRT provides improved accessibility, faster data acquisition, and spatially continuous thermal information that can support more efficient defect detection and condition assessment, thereby reducing inspection effort and lowering resource consumption.

However, the central findings of this review is that the full value of UAV-based thermal inspection can only be realized only when inspection outputs are integrated into structured digital environments such as BIM and DT platforms. Integrating thermal inspection data with digital models provides important advantages by enabling the spatial contextualization of detected anomalies, improved defect localization, and enhanced support for infrastructure monitoring and maintenance planning ([ 80 ,  93 ]; C. Zhang et al., [ 113 ] b), and lifecycle decision-making. Multimodal data fusion approaches combining thermal imagery with RGB imagery, photogrammetry, and LiDAR further enhance the interpretability and spatial mapping of inspection results [ 10 ,  20 ,  90 ]. These integrated workflows enable the creation of richer and more actionable digital representations of infrastructure assets, thereby forming a foundation for more advanced, data-driven asset management systems, which support more efficient maintenance strategies by enabling predictive maintenance and reducing unplanned repairs and material waste.

Despite these promising developments, several barriers still limit the transition from one-off thermal defect detection toward continuous monitoring and predictive maintenance. Technical barriers include sensor-resolution constraints, environmental sensitivity, calibration inconsistency, and uncertainty in thermal interpretation, all of which can affect the reliability of UAV-IRT inspection results [ 90 ,  91 ]. Data-integration barriers also remain significant, including inconsistent thermal metadata, interoperability limitations, heterogeneous data formats, and the difficulty of updating BIM and DT environments with recurring inspection data [ 52 ,  106 ]. Analytical barriers include the limited availability of ground-truth datasets, insufficient validation across different infrastructure materials and field conditions, and the need for more explainable AI outputs that can support engineering judgment [ 62 ]. In addition, organizational barriers such as implementation cost, regulatory constraints, data governance requirements, and the shortage of interdisciplinary expertise continue to restrict large-scale adoption within the AEC/FM industry [ 75 ]. These barriers indicate that future UAV-IRT research should move beyond defect detection alone and focus on producing reliable, interoperable, and decision-ready inspection information for lifecycle asset management.

To address these challenges, this review proposed a future research roadmap intended to guide the continued development of UAV-IRT with BIM and DT ecosystems. The roadmap highlights several key research priorities, including the development of standardized UAV-IRT inspection workflows, improved multimodal sensing integration, AI-enabled decision support systems, the expansion of DT applications toward larger infrastructure ecosystems, and stronger workforce training and education in digital inspection technologies. Progress in these areas will help enable more scalable and intelligent infrastructure monitoring systems capable of supporting predictive maintenance and lifecycle asset management, while also contributing to reduced resource consumption, lower lifecycle costs, and enhanced infrastructure resilience.

Overall, the integration of UAV-based thermographic inspection with BIM and DT technologies represents a promising pathway toward more intelligent, interoperable, and data-driven infrastructure management. Continued research and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential for transforming UAV-enabled inspection from isolated thermal observations into actionable knowledge that supports safer, more efficient, and more resilient built environments, ultimately advancing sustainable infrastructure systems and long-term asset performance.
